title: The Paschal mystery (CCC 571)
hookLine: his death and resurrection as one saving event

lines: A DARK CHURCH. A FIRE OUTSIDE.
A CROSS CUT INTO A CANDLE.
cards: Late on Holy Saturday night, a Catholic church is dark. Outside, a fire burns in a small iron bowl.
A priest cuts a cross into a tall new candle, then the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet, and the numbers of the year. He may press in five grains of incense, for five wounds.

The candle is lit from the fire and carried into the dark, and one by one every small candle is lit from it, until the whole room is gold. A cross, wounds, and light, all on one candle. Catholics refuse to separate them.

teach.b: Paschal comes from pascha, the Greek form of the Hebrew pesach: Passover. Jesus died at Passover, and the first Christians read his death through it. Paul, in the Douay-Rheims: "For Christ our pasch is sacrificed."

teach.h: ONE EVENT: THE CROSS AND THE RISING.
teach.b: The lamb whose blood marked the doors in Egypt, the night of passing from slavery to freedom: Christians saw Jesus as that lamb, and his death and rising as that passage. One event, not two.
The Catechism calls the cross and the resurrection together the Paschal mystery, and puts it at the center of the Good News. Good Friday isn't a sad chapter followed by a happy one.
It's one saving act: through death to life. That's why the liturgy treats Holy Thursday evening to Easter Sunday as one great celebration, the Triduum, the three days. Mystery.
In Catholic language, a mystery isn't a puzzle to solve.
It's something true and so deep you can keep entering it your whole life without reaching the bottom. The pattern.

teach.h: THE GRAIN OF WHEAT MUST DIE.
teach.b: Jesus gave it a picture beforehand: "unless the grain of wheat falling into the ground die, itself remaineth alone. But if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit."
Catholics say they are drawn into the Paschal mystery through baptism, and they recognize its shape in their own lives: endings that turn out to be passages, losses that bear fruit.
Not every sorrow feels that way while you're in it, and the Church doesn't pretend it does. It points at the candle: the cross is still on it, even in the light.

how: Catholics celebrate the Paschal mystery above all in the Easter Triduum, from Holy Thursday evening through Easter Sunday; at the Easter Vigil the Paschal candle is blessed, marked with a cross, alpha and omega, the year and five grains of incense, and lit from a new fire.

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.

s: Catholics treat Good Friday and Easter as two separate events
the Church calls the cross and resurrection together one Paschal mystery, one saving event.
the word paschal comes from the Passover
via Greek pascha, from the Hebrew pesach.
in Catholic language, a mystery is a puzzle waiting to be solved

games.q: some Greeks ask to see Jesus. he answers that his hour has come, and reaches for a picture from the fields. which one?
o: a grain of wheat that falls into the ground and dies.
a tree that never loses its leaves.
a harvest stored safely in a barn.
games.why: unless the grain of wheat die, it remains alone; if it dies, it bears much fruit. the shape of the Paschal mystery.

practice: If you have a crucifix and a candle nearby, set them side by side; if not, picture them, and look at the cross, then the light, then both at once.
Think of one ending in your own life that later became a beginning, a move, a loss, a no that led somewhere, and let it sit between the two. If you pray, you can thank God for it.

wordCard.voice: Paschal mystery. Christ's death and resurrection as one saving passage, named for the Passover, at the center of the Catholic faith.

orig.note: Greek: Passover, and Easter. borrowed from Aramaic and Hebrew pesach.
